title: THE BIBLE SAYS THEY TOOK WHICHEVER WOMEN THEY WANTED—AND THEN GOD SAW WHAT THE WORLD HAD BECOME.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE SAYS THEY TOOK WHICHEVER WOMEN THEY WANTED—AND THEN GOD SAW WHAT THE WORLD HAD BECOME.

Before the Flood, something terrifying was happening between power, desire, and the daughters of men. But the most disturbing part of Genesis 6 may not be who the “sons of God” were. It may be how much of that ancient world still looks like ours.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make you uncomfortable.
Not because God approved of what happened.
But because He wanted us to know it happened.
“They took them wives of all which they chose.” — Genesis 6:2, KJV
Read that again.
They saw women.
They desired them.
And they took whomever they chose.

The passage does not tell us that the women were consulted. It does not explicitly tell us that every union involved physical force, either. But the language is unsettling, especially when we discover what the world looked like just a few verses later.
Violence was spreading.
Human wickedness was multiplying.
And the thoughts of the human heart had become continually evil.
Then came the Flood.
But here is the question that has troubled readers for centuries.
Who were these men? Who were these women? And what exactly was happening on earth before God brought judgment upon the ancient world?
Some believe fallen angels were involved.
Others believe powerful human rulers were taking women as they pleased.
Still others understand the passage as describing the collapse of the distinction between those who worshiped God and those who rejected Him.
The disagreement is ancient.
The consequences described in Scripture are terrifying.
And buried beneath the mystery is a warning about the human heart that we cannot afford to ignore.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about an ancient Bible passage is discovering that the world it describes does not feel ancient at all.
Genesis 6 begins almost quietly.
Humanity was multiplying across the earth. Daughters were being born. Families were growing. Civilization was developing.
From the outside, life might have appeared to be progressing.
But something was deeply wrong.
Genesis 6:2 says:
“That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.”
The original Hebrew makes the scene even more worth examining.
The phrase בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים (bene ha-elohim) means “sons of God” or, more literally, “sons of the God/divine being,” depending on how the expression is understood in context.
The phrase בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם (benot ha-adam) means “daughters of humankind.”
And then come the words that demand our attention.
וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ
Vayyiqchu lahem nashim mikkol asher bacharu.
A close translation is:
“And they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.”
Notice the emphasis.
They saw.
They chose.
They took.
The Hebrew verb laqach, here appearing as vayyiqchu, means “they took.” It is also used elsewhere for taking a wife and does not, by itself, prove abduction or rape.
That distinction matters.
We must never force Scripture to say more than it says, even when the subject is disturbing.
But we must also refuse to soften what the wider passage reveals.
Genesis is describing a world moving toward catastrophic moral corruption.
And the repeated emphasis on what these figures wanted and chose raises a serious question about desire unconstrained by righteousness.
Who were these “sons of God”?
Here is where the mystery deepens.
In Job 1:6 and Job 2:1, the expression “sons of God” appears in scenes involving heavenly beings presenting themselves before the LORD. Job 38:7 also uses similar language in a heavenly context.
Because of these passages, many ancient Jewish interpreters understood Genesis 6 as referring to heavenly beings who crossed a forbidden boundary.
This interpretation became especially prominent in the ancient Jewish work known as 1 Enoch.
According to that tradition, rebellious heavenly beings descended, took human women, and produced extraordinary offspring.
But we need to be careful.

The Book of 1 Enoch is important evidence of ancient interpretation, but its status as Scripture differs among Christian traditions. It should not automatically be treated as having the same authority as Genesis.
The Bible itself does not explicitly identify the “sons of God” in Genesis 6 as fallen angels.

Some Christians connect this passage with Jude 6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4–5, where sinful angels and divine judgment are discussed. Yet those connections are interpreted differently by faithful Bible scholars.
There is also a serious difficulty.
In Matthew 22:30, Jesus says that angels in heaven do not marry.

Some understand His words as an objection to the angelic interpretation. Others point out that Jesus specifically speaks about angels in heaven, not about what rebellious spiritual beings might attempt.
Neither argument settles every question.
A second major interpretation understands the “sons of God” as descendants of Seth, the family line associated with calling upon the name of the LORD in Genesis 4:26.
Under this view, the passage describes the corruption of a godly community through marriages shaped by attraction rather than covenant faithfulness.
There is a third interpretation as well.
Some scholars understand the “sons of God” as ancient kings, aristocrats, or powerful rulers who claimed extraordinary status and accumulated women according to their own desires.
In ancient royal societies, power could become a license for exploitation.
A ruler could decide that wanting something was reason enough to possess it.
And the powerless could suffer beneath that entitlement.
This interpretation takes seriously the disturbing language of taking wives “from all whom they chose.”
Yet it, too, remains debated.
The honest conclusion is that Genesis 6:1–4 does not provide enough information to establish one interpretation beyond all reasonable disagreement.
And perhaps that is where we need to confront something about ourselves.
We can become so fascinated by the identity of the mysterious beings that we overlook the unmistakable moral condition of the world surrounding them.
We want to know whether angels came down.
God wants us to see how far humanity had fallen.
We want to solve the mystery of the Nephilim.
God shows us a world where evil was becoming ordinary.
We want the extraordinary details.
But the ordinary sins may be the ones standing closest to our own front doors.
Think about that.
How many people today still believe that having power gives them the right to take what they want?
How many relationships are destroyed because desire becomes more important than faithfulness?
How many vulnerable people are treated as possessions rather than human beings made in God's image?
How many people are admired for their influence while the wounds they leave behind remain hidden?
The ancient world may have looked different.
The human heart has not changed nearly as much as we would like to believe.
And that brings us to another strange word.
Nephilim.
Genesis 6:4 says:

“There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” — KJV
The Hebrew word is נְפִלִים (nephilim).
The King James Version translates it as “giants,” reflecting an ancient interpretive tradition also associated with the Greek Septuagint.
But the precise meaning of Nephilim remains uncertain.
Some associate the word with the Hebrew root naphal, meaning “to fall,” although the etymology is debated.
Others emphasize the description of these figures as mighty men of ancient renown.
The Hebrew expression gibborim refers to mighty or powerful men, often warriors.
And anshei hashem describes men of name or reputation.
Men remembered.
Men celebrated.
Men whose names carried weight.
But there is something deeply sobering here.
A person can be famous on earth and still stand condemned before heaven.
A person can have extraordinary strength and possess no righteousness.
A person can command the admiration of an entire generation while living in rebellion against God.
The world may celebrate power.
God examines the heart.
The world may remember your name.
God knows what you did when nobody was watching.
And suddenly Genesis 6 becomes painfully personal.
Because we live in a generation that knows how to manufacture fame.
We know how to make people appear powerful.
We know how to celebrate wealth, beauty, influence, and dominance.
But none of those things can cleanse a guilty conscience.
None can reconcile a sinner to a holy God.
None can purchase forgiveness.
A thousand people may applaud the life you are living.
But applause is not absolution.
And reputation is not redemption.
Then the story takes a devastating turn.
Genesis 6:5 says:
“And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
Pause over those words.
GOD saw.
Not merely what humanity was doing publicly.
Not merely the violence people could observe.
Not merely the corruption that had become impossible to hide.
God saw the thoughts.
The intentions.
The inner life.
The things human beings could conceal from one another but never from their Creator.
The Hebrew phrase יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ (yetser machshevot libbo) concerns the formation or inclination of the thoughts of the heart.
The diagnosis was not merely that people occasionally made bad decisions.
The moral corruption had reached the very intentions of the heart.
And this should humble every one of us.
Because it is possible to look respectable while nurturing something destructive inside.
It is possible to speak kindly in public while secretly planning revenge.
It is possible to appear religious while feeding pride, lust, greed, bitterness, or cruelty.
It is possible to know the language of holiness without surrendering the hidden places of the soul to God.
Jesus would later expose this same problem.
In Mark 7:21–23, He teaches that evil thoughts and sinful actions proceed from within the human heart.
He does not allow us to blame everything on society.
He does not allow us to hide behind religious appearances.
He goes deeper.
To the place where sin begins.
And if we are willing to be honest, that is where this story stops being merely about the people before the Flood.
It becomes about us.
Not because every person is guilty of the particular atrocities that characterized Noah's generation.
But because every one of us needs the mercy of God.
Every one of us has sinned.
Every one of us needs a Savior.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That includes the respectable.
The religious.
The successful.
The broken.
The person who has spent years hiding behind a smile.
And the person reading these words who knows there is something in their life they have not yet surrendered to Jesus.
You may have convinced everyone around you that you are fine.
But God sees the heart.
And here is the astonishing truth.
The God who sees what you are hiding is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
He does not need you to manufacture a spotless past.
He calls you to turn from sin and come to the Savior who died for sinners.
But before we reach that hope, we must face the seriousness of what happened in Noah's day.
Genesis 6:6 says that the LORD was grieved in His heart.
Think about the weight of that statement.
The Creator looked upon a world filled with human beings made in His image.
Human beings created for relationship with Him.
Human beings entrusted with life, responsibility, and the capacity to reflect His goodness.
And the world had become filled with wickedness.
Scripture uses the language of divine grief to communicate the profound seriousness of humanity's rebellion. It does not mean God was surprised or had lost control.
The world was not merely making mistakes.
It was defying the goodness of its Creator.
Then Genesis 6:11 gives another terrible description:
“The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.”
The Hebrew word translated “violence” is חָמָס (chamas or ḥāmās).
It carries the sense of violence, wrongdoing, and destructive injustice.
This is one of the clearest descriptions of the world before the Flood.
Not simply mysterious marriages.
Not merely powerful figures.
Not just ancient giants.
Violence.
Corruption.
Human evil spreading through society.
And God did not treat it as insignificant.
That matters because some people have been wounded so deeply that they wonder whether heaven notices.
The person who was betrayed.
The woman whose dignity was disregarded.
The child who grew up afraid.
The believer who watched someone powerful escape earthly consequences.
The person who prayed for justice and wondered whether God had gone silent.
Genesis reminds us that evil does not become righteous merely because it becomes common.
God sees.
God knows.
And His judgment is not an embarrassment to His goodness.
It is an expression of His holiness.
But we must also remember that divine judgment is not permission for us to become cruel.
The God who condemns violence does not authorize us to mistreat people in His name.
The God who sees injustice calls His people to righteousness, mercy, and truth.
And then, in the middle of one of the darkest chapters of human history, Scripture gives us seven words that change the atmosphere of the entire story.
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.” — Genesis 6:8, KJV
There it is.
Grace.
In Hebrew, the word is חֵן (chen or ḥen).
Favor.
Grace.
A beautiful word appearing against a terrifying background.
The earth was corrupt.
Violence was everywhere.
Judgment was approaching.
But Noah found grace.
Do not rush past that sentence.
The story does not say that Noah built a ladder tall enough to escape judgment by his own strength.
It does not say that human achievement could cancel the world's guilt.
It says Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
Genesis 6:9 also describes Noah as righteous and blameless among his contemporaries, a man who walked with God.
His life was marked by faith and obedience.
Hebrews 11:7 later explains that Noah acted by faith when God warned him about things not yet seen.
And through faith, Noah prepared the ark.
Imagine the scene.
A man building a vessel in obedience to a divine warning.
The world continuing around him.
People living their ordinary lives.
Families gathering.
Meals being prepared.
Plans being made.
And judgment drawing nearer.
Jesus Himself refers to this in Matthew 24:37–39.
He says that as the days of Noah were, so would be the coming of the Son of Man.
People were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until Noah entered the ark.
Then the Flood came.
Notice something important.
Eating is not evil.
Drinking is not inherently evil.
Marriage is not evil.
These are ordinary parts of human life.
The warning is not that normal activities are sinful.
It is that people can become so absorbed in ordinary life that they remain unprepared for God's judgment.
They can be busy building a future while neglecting eternity.
They can plan weddings and never consider their Creator.
They can pursue success while ignoring the condition of their souls.
They can have everything scheduled except repentance.
And that is a warning for our generation.
We know how to fill our calendars.
We know how to pursue careers.
We know how to build online identities.
We know how to make long-term plans.
But how often do we seriously ask whether we are walking with God?
How often do we examine our hearts before Scripture?
How often do we repent instead of defending ourselves?
How often do we treat Jesus as Lord rather than merely as someone we mention when life becomes difficult?
Perhaps the most dangerous form of spiritual sleep is not openly rejecting God.
Perhaps it is becoming so comfortable with life that we no longer feel the urgency of responding to Him.
And here is where the story becomes even more extraordinary.
The ark was not the final answer to human sin.
It was a real instrument of preservation in Noah's generation, but the Bible's story does not end with Noah stepping onto dry ground.
Because the Flood did not remove sin from the human heart forever.
After the waters receded, humanity still needed redemption.
Genesis 8:21 acknowledges the continuing evil inclination of the human heart.
The world needed something greater than another beginning.
It needed a Savior.
And that Savior is Jesus Christ.

The apostle Peter draws a connection between Noah's deliverance through water and Christian baptism in 1 Peter 3:20–21, emphasizing that salvation is grounded in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, not in the mere washing of dirt from the body.
The point is not that Noah's ark and Jesus are identical in every detail.
It is that the same God who judges sin also provides salvation according to His mercy and promises.
And in Jesus Christ, God's saving purpose reaches its glorious fulfillment.
Jesus did not come merely to improve human behavior.
He came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The cross reveals something the world before the Flood desperately needed to understand.
God does not overlook evil.
But His mercy is greater than the worst past of anyone who truly comes to Christ in repentance and faith.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.
The Savior does not call sin harmless.
He bears its terrible cost.
He does not offer us permission to continue in darkness.
He calls us into the light.
He does not simply promise a better reputation.
He offers reconciliation with God.
That is why 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that your past never happened.
Not that your wounds were imaginary.
Not that your choices carried no consequences.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem what sin has devastated and transform those who surrender to Him.
From rebellion to repentance.
From condemnation to forgiveness.
From spiritual death to new life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your story has never involved public scandal.
Maybe nobody knows what you have done.
Maybe the battle is happening entirely inside your heart.
A secret addiction.
A hidden relationship.
A bitterness you have carried for years.
A compromise you keep excusing.
A religious appearance that no longer matches your private life.
Or maybe you are not the one who inflicted the wound.
Maybe you are the person who has been carrying it.
Someone used their authority against you.
Someone treated your trust as something disposable.
Someone made you feel powerless.
Someone convinced you that your worth depended on what they wanted from you.
Hear this clearly.
You were never created to be someone else's possession.
You bear the image of God.
Your dignity is not determined by another person's desires.
And the evil done against you is not evidence that God approved of it.
Jesus welcomes the weary and burdened.
He sees the overlooked.
He calls the brokenhearted toward His healing presence.
He is not indifferent to injustice.
And He is not powerless to redeem.
Healing may involve time, wise support, accountability, and the courage to seek safety. Faith does not require you to remain in an abusive situation.
The Gospel never asks us to call darkness light.
It calls us to bring darkness into the presence of Christ.
And for those who have been the ones causing harm, the invitation is equally serious.
Repent.
Not merely because you fear consequences.
Not merely because your reputation is threatened.
But because sin is rebellion against a holy God and destructive to people He loves.
True repentance is more than saying sorry.
It involves turning from sin, telling the truth, and bearing the fruit of a changed life.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant abuse.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves and transforms sinners through Jesus Christ.
And if that truth exposes something you have been hiding, perhaps today is the day to stop running.
Not toward public performance.
Not toward religious appearances.
Toward Jesus.
Your honesty may help another person realize they do not have to face their struggle alone.
There is one more detail in the story of Noah that we cannot afford to miss.
The ark had a door.
Genesis 7:16 tells us that the LORD shut Noah in.
The moment of entering had passed.
The judgment came.
And those outside could not reverse what had happened.
We should be careful not to invent conversations or dramatic scenes that Scripture does not record.
The Bible does not describe people pounding on the ark or Noah pleading through its walls.
But it does tell us that the Flood came and that those outside the ark perished.
The warning is solemn enough without embellishment.
And Jesus Himself tells us to be ready.
Not because He delights in terrifying people.
But because eternity matters.
Because sin is serious.
Because judgment is real.
And because the invitation of the Gospel is too precious to ignore.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an astonishing promise.
The same Scriptures that warn us about judgment also reveal a Savior who welcomes those who come to Him.
You may be carrying shame.
Come to Him.
You may have spent years resisting His voice.
Come to Him.
You may have convinced yourself that you are too far gone.
Come to Him.
You may have a thousand questions about Genesis 6 and the mysterious beings described there.
Bring those questions too.
But do not allow fascination with the mysteries of Scripture to distract you from its clearest invitation.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
The greatest question is not whether the Nephilim were giants.
It is whether you know the Savior.
Not whether ancient powerful men were admired.
But whether your own heart belongs to Christ.
Not whether you can explain every mystery before the Flood.
But whether you are ready to meet the Lord.
Because the Bible was not given merely to satisfy our curiosity about ancient darkness.
It was given to reveal the truth of God and lead us toward the salvation found in Jesus Christ.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn Scripture into entertainment.
Not to manufacture fear.
Not to exploit suffering for attention.
But to bring the Word of God into a world where so many people are spiritually exhausted, confused, wounded, and hungry for truth.
Every article we share is an opportunity for someone to encounter Scripture.
Every biblical resource is an opportunity for a believer to grow deeper.
Every testimony of repentance is a reminder that Christ is still transforming lives.
And every person who helps carry the Gospel forward becomes part of something that reaches beyond one post, one page, or one generation.
Not simply to increase its reach.
Invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the person who has drifted from church, and even the skeptic who is willing to examine what Scripture actually says.
Truth should be shared with love, not used as a weapon.
And for those who want to do more than read, there is an opportunity to help sustain this ministry.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
And we want to give something back.
Those resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, deepen their faith, strengthen their prayer lives, and grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
And they remain FREE.
Because the Word of God should never be reduced to a sales pitch.
That is the beauty of voluntary generosity.
Someone gives.
Someone else receives encouragement.
Someone opens a Bible.
Someone begins asking questions.
Someone who thought God had abandoned them hears about the grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps a life begins to change.
Jesus Christ is not looking for customers.
He calls people to become His disciples.
And His grace cannot be purchased.
It is received through faith.
So if you have reached the end of this article, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Genesis 6 begins with people taking whatever they desired.
It moves into a world filled with corruption and violence.
It confronts us with the holiness of God.
But in the middle of judgment, we encounter the extraordinary words:
“But Noah found grace.”
That is not an invitation to presume upon God's patience.
It is an invitation to take His mercy seriously.
The world before the Flood reminds us that human power cannot save us.
Human fame cannot save us.
Human pleasure cannot save us.
Human achievement cannot save us.
Only God can save.
And the Gospel announces that salvation has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
The One who died for our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who makes all things new.
If God examined the direction of your heart today, what would He find?
Would He find a life surrendered to Jesus?
Or a life that has become skilled at hiding from Him?
You do not have to answer that publicly.
But you do need to answer honestly before God.
If this article helped you understand the Bible more deeply, share what stood out to you. Your question or testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs.
Then take that next step of faith.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Seek fellowship with faithful believers.
Make peace where repentance requires it.
Seek help where healing requires it.
And keep your eyes on Jesus Christ.
Because the most important part of this story was never the mystery of the mighty men.
It was the mercy of the mighty God.
The world before the Flood teaches us how far the human heart can fall. The cross of Jesus Christ reveals how far God's love went to redeem sinners.
And if you remember only one thing from everything you have read, remember this:
The God who saw the darkness before the Flood can see the darkness you hide today—and through Jesus Christ, He still calls you out of it and into His marvelous light.
